common_name: Dr. Dormon Louisiana Iris (Wild Orchid and Dahlia Mauve Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Sidney Conger registered Dr. Dormon in 1972, naming it for Louisiana naturalist Caroline Dormon; it opens wild-orchid-toned standards above dahlia-mauve falls marked with a signal patch, on stalks reaching about 38 inches and blooming late in the season. Henry Rowlan later used it as a parent, crossed with 'Black Gamecock', to breed the fuchsia-purple Voodoo Magic. Grow it in full sun with rich, constantly moist to wet soil typical of Louisiana iris culture, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Mikal Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Mary Dunn bred and registered Mikal in 1980 from a seedling cross with 'Myra Arny', and Bay View Gardens introduced it the following year; it bears ruffled blue flowers on a yellow-green signal and earned an Honorable Mention in 1984. Mikal later served as a parent, crossed with 'Clara Goula', in breeding the orange-signaled C'est La Mote. Give it full sun and steady wet-to-moist soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Koorawatha Louisiana Iris (Yellow Gold Iris with Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Australian hybridizer John C. Taylor registered Koorawatha in 1984, a yellow-gold Louisiana iris with a green throat marked by a darker golden center line; it went on to win the Australian Dykes Medal. It was later crossed with 'Lucile Holley' to produce the pink-magenta and cream Dazzling Star. Keep it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigor.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Bushfire Moon Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Orange-Yellow Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Heather Pryor registered Bushfire Moon in 1994 from a cross of 'Alluvial Gold' and 'Gladiator's Gift'; it opens ruffled orange-yellow flowers with a fine green line signal on all petals and collected regional trial awards in New South Wales before earning recognition as a top single bloom. Pryor later used it, crossed with 'Lucy Payens', to breed the early-blooming, peach-toned Peaches In Wine. Grow it in full sun and rich, constantly wet soil, and expect bloom to open earlier in the season than many Louisiana cultivars.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Lucy Payens Louisiana Iris (Breeding Line Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Lucy Payens is a Louisiana iris cultivar chiefly known today through its use in breeding lines, including as a parent alongside 'Bushfire Moon' in Heather Pryor's early-blooming Peaches In Wine, which pairs peach-toned standards with deep red falls. Like other Louisiana cultivars of its generation it performs best with the species' standard culture. Grow it in full sun with rich, constantly wet to consistently moist soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Guessing Game Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Pale Mauve Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: John C. Taylor registered Guessing Game in 1994, a tall Louisiana iris reaching nearly 5 feet with ruffled pale mauve flowers veined and dotted blue-violet, centered on a green line signal surrounded by pale cream. Hooker Nichols later crossed it with 'Heather Pryor' to breed the salmon-raspberry Watermelon Wizard. Plant it in full sun with consistently wet soil, staking tall stalks if needed in exposed sites.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Heather Pryor Louisiana Iris (Cream and Pink Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: John C. Taylor registered this tall, heavily ruffled Louisiana iris in 1993 and named it for fellow Australian hybridizer Heather Pryor; cream standards and falls are veined and flushed pink toward a paler rim, with a green line signal surrounded by a yellow center area, opening late midseason on stalks over 4 feet tall. Hooker Nichols later crossed it with 'Guessing Game' to breed the salmon-raspberry Watermelon Wizard. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil typical of Louisiana iris culture.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Mighty Rich Louisiana Iris (Velvety Ruby Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Charles Arny registered Mighty Rich in 1982, a velvety ruby-red Louisiana iris with huge bright yellow signals bold enough to spot from a distance across the garden. Florida breeder John C. Taylor later crossed it with 'Clara Goula' to produce the light pink and salmon bitone All Aglaze, registered in 1989. Plant it in full sun with reliably moist to wet soil through the bloom period for the deepest color saturation.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Dural Bluebird Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Australian hybridizer John C. Taylor registered Dural Bluebird in 1993, a nicely ruffled blue Louisiana iris named for his Dural garden district. Texas hybridizer Ron Killingsworth later crossed it with 'Hush Money' to breed Our Friend Dick, a tall pink-violet and dark violet bitone named for a fellow iris enthusiast. Give it full sun and steady wet-to-moist soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Hush Money Louisiana Iris (Cream with Blue-Cast Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Mary Dunn and Joseph Ghio registered Hush Money in 1998; cream standards carry a faint blue cast above cream falls marked by a raised gold line signal, opening midseason on stalks about 3 feet tall, and the cultivar earned an Honorable Mention in 2002. Texas hybridizer Ron Killingsworth later crossed it with 'Dural Bluebird' to breed the tall pink-violet and dark violet bitone Our Friend Dick. Give it full sun and steady moisture, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Creole Flame Louisiana Iris (Dark Cardinal Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Carl Wyatt registered Creole Flame in 1973, a dark cardinal red Louisiana iris that earned an Honorable Mention in 1975. Mary Dunn later crossed it with 'Monument' to breed Rhett, a mahogany red cultivar that went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 1991. Plant it in full sun with rich, consistently wet soil for the strongest color saturation on its upright stems.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Bellocq Louisiana Iris (Salmon Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Patrick O'Connor registered Bellocq in 2007, a compact Louisiana iris standing only 20 to 22 inches tall with salmon-colored standards and falls, blooming midseason. O'Connor later crossed it with 'Percolator' to breed When Pigs Fly, whose flowers open pale amber and fade to soft pearl white; Bellocq has also been used as a parent, together with Lemon Zest, in breeding Chief Of Chiefs. Site it in full sun with rich, wet soil typical of Louisiana iris culture.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Percolator Louisiana Iris (Ochre and Nasturtium Orange Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: T. J. Betts registered Percolator in 2001 from a cross of 'Dural Gold' and 'Amanda's Echo'; it bears ochre standards infused with grey above pale nasturtium-orange falls veined in maroon, centered on a yellow steeple signal, opening late on tall stalks over 3 feet. Patrick O'Connor later crossed it with 'Bellocq' to breed the pale amber and pearl-white When Pigs Fly. Site it in full sun with rich, wet soil, and expect one of the latest bloom times among Louisiana cultivars.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Tarnished Brass Louisiana Iris (Historic Breeding Line Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Frank Chowning registered Tarnished Brass in the early 1960s, a historic Louisiana iris now known chiefly through its role as a parent in later breeding. Henry Rowlan crossed it in 1983 with a terra-cotta-toned form of the wild species Iris fulva to produce the scarlet red, fall-reblooming Red Echo. Grow it in full sun in reliably wet to consistently moist soil in the same conditions favored by its Louisiana iris descendants.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Castalia Bearded Iris (Historic 1933 Fragrant Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Castalia is a historically significant early-1930s tall bearded iris and an ancestor of later Dykes Medal-winning dark blue bearded iris.

directions: R. Williamson registered Castalia in 1933, a strongly fragrant tall bearded iris descended from 'Oriflamme' that earned an Honorable Mention in 1936. Paul Cook later used it, crossed with 'Santa Barbara' and then 'Great Lakes', to breed Distance, a silvery light blue iris that became an important early ancestor in the lineage behind later Dykes Medal-winning dark blue bearded iris. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage to avoid rot.

common_name: Classic Treasure Bearded Iris (Breeding Line Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Classic Treasure is part of hybridizer Fred Kerr's series of 'Treasure'-named tall bearded iris introductions. Kerr crossed it with 'Glistening Icicle' to produce the white, blue-edged border bearded iris Christiana Baker, registered in 1999. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil, planting rhizomes shallowly and dividing every three to four years.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Glistening Icicle Bearded Iris (White with True Blue Falls)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: William Maryott registered Glistening Icicle in 1982 from a cross of 'Full Tide' and 'President Farnsworth'; it carries white standards above smooth, heavily ruffled medium true-blue falls, opening midseason on 3-foot stalks and earning an Honorable Mention in 1986, with reported rebloom in California, Missouri, and the Netherlands. Fred Kerr crossed it with 'Classic Treasure' to breed Christiana Baker, a white border bearded iris with blue-edged falls registered in 1999. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Desert Jewel Louisiana Iris (Brown Gold Marbled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: John C. Taylor registered Desert Jewel in 1991, a brown-gold Louisiana iris with standards marbled gold, now valued mainly as a parent behind several later registered cultivars including Better Believe It and Ann Horden. Heather Pryor crossed it with 'Gladiator's Gift' to breed the heavily ruffled, tomato-red Hot And Spicy, which went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal. Full sun brings out the richest tones, and the plant tolerates the wet, humid conditions of Gulf Coast bayou gardens well.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Van Cliburn Bearded Iris (Historic 1961 Medium Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Cliff Benson registered Van Cliburn in 1961 from seedling 58-5C, a large, bold medium blue self with domed standards and semi-flared, thick-substanced falls on stalks over 3 feet tall. It was the final parent in a cross culminating in Skywatch, registered in 1963, an immense, extremely smooth lavender-blue self that went on to win the American Dykes Medal in 1970. Divide every three to four years after bloom, and set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil.

common_name: Vermilion Queen Louisiana Iris (Pale Cream and Buttery Gold Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Richard Goula registered Vermilion Queen in 1992 from a cross of 'Clara Goula' and 'Gold Plaque'; despite the name, its pale cream standards and medium buttery-gold falls carry a greenish-gold signal and a slight spicy fragrance, opening in early midseason on 3-foot stalks. Kevin Vaughn later crossed it with 'Heavenly Glow' to breed the lemon-yellow Lemon Zest, winner of the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2019. Site it in full sun with steady moisture typical of Louisiana iris culture.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Heavenly Glow Louisiana Iris (Orange-Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Richard Morgan registered Heavenly Glow in 1988, an orange-red Louisiana iris with a green-yellow steeple signal and green style arms, the orange signal rimmed by a darker red that echoes the veining on the falls. Kevin Vaughn later crossed it with 'Vermilion Queen' to breed the lemon-yellow, electric-green-signaled Lemon Zest, winner of the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal. Site it in full sun with steady moisture, since the warm color intensifies when the rhizomes never dry out between waterings.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)
